strengths: Addresses well-motivated and practically important problem of concept shift detection and attribution, particularly relevant in healthcare where shifts have clear scientific implications
Strong empirical results: SGShift achieves AUC > 0.9 and recall > 90% across semi-synthetic and real experiments, typically 2-3x better than baselines
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 16 model configurations, semi-synthetic ground truth validation, real-world results validated against medical literature (e.g., COVID-19 Omicron findings)
Solid theoretical contributions: Theorem 4.1 provides convergence guarantees for GAM estimation with offset terms, and Lemma 4.2 rigorously extends knockoffs to provide both PFER and FDR control
Interpretability focus: Using GAMs as transparent update terms is valuable, enabling interpretation even when base models are black-box
Good reproducibility: Code available in supplement, detailed preprocessing for each dataset, all hyperparameters specified, multiple public datasets with fetching code for restricted data
Convincing real-world validation: Figure 2 demonstrates that true concept shifts in practice are indeed sparse with characteristic elbow shapes, supporting core assumption
weaknesses: Critical ambiguity about basis function selection: The paper never explains how φ(X) are chosen in practice (splines, polynomials, automated selection?), despite this being central to both theory and implementation, severely limiting reproducibility

Restrictive modeling assumption that concept shift can be represented as linear combinations of fixed basis functions is strong and never validated empirically; authors claim good performance 'even when this assumption falters' but provide no evidence or analysis

Limited methodological novelty: GAMs, L1 regularization, and knockoffs are established techniques; core contribution (adding sparse correction term) is relatively straightforward; Theorem 4.1 is incremental adaptation of standard lasso analysis

Narrow experimental scope: only 3 real datasets, all from healthcare domain; tabular data only; semi-synthetic setup uses additive perturbations potentially favoring an additive shift model; no comparison to SJS [CZZ22] despite similar scope
Missing practical guidance: method identifies shifted features but provides no guidance on downstream use (retraining, reweighting) or demonstration that identified features enable model improvement

Unclear basis function handling for mixed data types: while Model-X knockoffs require i.i.d. features and construction details are non-trivial for categorical variables in healthcare, these challenges are not addressed
Hyperparameter selection not discussed: unclear how λ is chosen (grid search, cross-validation?), and sensitivity to B, π choices for knockoffs is not analyzed
Large confidence intervals in aggregated results (Figure 1) may obscure concerning performance variation; individual model results in appendix show more consistent patterns but receive less emphasis

Strong sparsity assumption without guidance on failure modes: authors acknowledge dense shifts 'may exist and be difficult to explain' but provide no method to detect when shifts are too dense or analysis of graceful degradation

Unclear comparison to baselines: WhyShift is claimed as 'directly comparable' but methods are substantially different (separate model training vs. explicit shift modeling); comparison setup and fair baseline configuration not fully detailed

strengths: Addresses a practically important problem: identifying which features cause concept shift in distribution shift scenarios
Provides theoretical guarantees on convergence (Theorem 4.1) and FDR control (Lemma 4.2) for the proposed methods
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple settings: 16 model configurations, 3 datasets, matched/mismatched scenarios, and sample size sensitivity analysis
Achieves strong empirical results with AUC > 0.9 and recall > 90% on semi-synthetic data, substantially outperforming weak baselines
Practical extensions (SGShift-A for model misspecification, SGShift-K for false discovery control) show thoughtful design
Real-world COVID-19 results align with medical literature, suggesting practical validity
Extensive supplementary materials with code and detailed experimental setup support reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: combines L1-regularized GAM, knockoffs, and stability selection—all well-established techniques—without substantial new theoretical insights; Theorem 4.1 is a straightforward adaptation of standard Lasso analysis
Critical baseline missing: No comparison with SJS [CZZ22], which directly targets sparse shift identification; this is the most relevant existing method but is absent from experiments
Weak baseline design: Diff is a strawman (simple outcome regression), SHAP adaptation is unfair (not designed for this task), limiting confidence in superiority claims

Sparsity assumption insufficiently justified: Central assumption that concept shifts are sparse is empirically validated but lacks theoretical analysis; no guidance on when shifts will be dense versus sparse
Basis function specification missing: What are φ(X) in practice (polynomial features? splines?)? Not clearly specified. Without this, reproducibility and practical application are compromised
Hyperparameter selection guidance absent: No principled procedure for choosing K (number of basis functions), λ, λ_ω, λ_δ, or π; practitioners lack implementation guidance
Conflicting modeling assumptions: Assumes source model f̂(X) ≈ f(X), yet concept shift indicates f̂ is misspecified; interaction between f̂ error and δ estimation unanalyzed

Ground truth validation limited: Semi-synthetic shift generation may favor the method; real-world validation (Figures 2-3) lacks true ground truth about shifted features; loss recovery curves show diminishing returns but don't prove feature selection correctness
Narrow scope: Restricted to tabular data and healthcare domain only; all 3 real datasets are healthcare; generalization and scope unclear

Insufficient empirical analysis: No ablation on K, basis functions, or regularization choices; no statistical significance testing on Table 2; knockoff construction for basis function space not detailed; no computational cost comparison
Missing practical sensitivity analysis: How sensitive are results to basis function choice and K selection? No systematic study provided

strengths: Clear problem formulation addressing a distinct gap in distribution shift literature - attributing concept shift to sparse feature sets is novel and well-motivated
Sound methodology combining GAMs as sparse updates with established feature selection techniques; the absorption term for handling model misspecification is principled
Rigorous theoretical guarantees: Theorem 4.1 provides convergence bounds, and Lemma 4.2 properly extends knockoff FDR control to the two-model difference setting

Comprehensive experimental evaluation with ground truth semi-synthetic data across 16 model configurations, demonstrating consistent and substantial improvements (AUC >0.9, recall 80-90% vs. 64-82% for baselines)
Strong empirical validation of sparsity assumption (Figure 2) on real data showing characteristic elbow behavior, with COVID-19 example validated against medical literature
Excellent reproducibility: code and data provided, detailed hyperparameters, complete proofs; evaluation across multiple models and datasets
Natural extensions to standard feature selection tools (ℓ1 regularization and knockoffs) with elegant integration of FDR/PFER control
weaknesses: Strong structural assumptions inadequately justified: assumes shift decomposable as ϕ(X)^T δ with linear combinations of K fixed basis functions, but K selection, basis function choice, and sensitivity to these choices not addressed despite being critical
Sparsity assumption validated only on three healthcare datasets with no systematic analysis of robustness when shifts are dense, partially sparse, or nonlinear
Limited real-world validation: only healthcare domain, three related datasets, and qualitative validation (COVID-19 example lacks ground truth shifted features for quantitative verification)

Ad-hoc baseline comparison with WhyShift adapted by extracting features from tree paths, raising fairness concerns; no empirical comparison with conceptually similar Sparse Joint Shift (CZZ22) despite discussing it
Hyperparameter selection under-specified: no guidance provided for choosing λ, λ_ω, λ_δ, or stability selection parameters π and B; cross-validation procedure not described
Method restricted to tabular data only; applicability to non-tabular domains (images, sequences, graphs) unknown despite distribution shifts occurring frequently in these modalities
Model quality dependence: results depend on source model fit; sensitivity to poor-fitting source models not fully explored despite motivation for absorption term
Missing failure case analysis: no characterization of which shift patterns are hardest to detect or systematic analysis of when method fails

strengths: Novel and practical problem formulation: Reformulating concept shift diagnosis as learning a sparse correction to a source model elegantly avoids error accumulation of plugin approaches and provides an interpretable framework.

Solid theoretical contributions: Theorems 3.1-3.3 provide estimation consistency and FDR control guarantees, with the key advantage of allowing ET[Y|X] to be nonparametric while only requiring well-specification of the correction form.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 48 semi-synthetic settings across 3 datasets with systematic testing of sparse/dense shifts, varying sample sizes, and complex scenarios (high-dimensional, correlated features, low SNR); consistent 0.1-0.2 AUC improvements over baselines.

Strong real-data validation: COVID-19 case study correctly identifies respiratory failure reduction with Omicron (validated against medical literature); Lupus ancestry study identifies eQTL-backed genes; large-scale ACS validation on 87 cases shows sparsity holds empirically.

Practical and flexible methodology: Three variants (SGShift, SGShift-A, SGShift-K) provide options for prediction correction, feature selection, and FDR-controlled selection; handles source model misspecification through absorption term.

Robustness to assumption violations: Despite assuming sparsity, method maintains strong performance (AUC >0.8) in dense shift settings and with high feature correlation, suggesting practical resilience beyond theory.
Sample efficiency: Demonstrates ability to identify >50% of shifted features with only 100 target-domain samples (SGShift-K in Figure 1), enabling practical online learning applications.
weaknesses: Theory-practice gap: Theorem 3.1 only guarantees estimation consistency, not exact support recovery. No theoretical explanation for why method performs well in dense shift settings (Table 1) where sparsity assumption is violated, though empirical robustness is demonstrated.

Limited technical novelty: Core contribution is applying L1-regularized GAM to a correction term—a straightforward combination of existing techniques. Knockoff application directly adapts Candès et al. (2018); SGShift-A's hierarchical regularization is pragmatic but not deeply novel.

Incomplete experimental comparisons: Missing comparisons with Singh et al. (2024, 2025), Chen et al. (2022), and Zhang et al. (2023) despite citing these as related work addressing similar problems; limited to 3 baselines (Diff, WhyShift, SHAP).

Methodological parameter choices lack justification: Lambda selection via cross-validation for feature selection (not prediction) may be suboptimal; hierarchical regularization parameter c chosen from range 0.1-0.9 without principled guidance; knockoff aggregation requires specifying B without practical guidance.

Scope limitations: Restricted to tabular data; requires labeled target domain data (unlike unlabeled methods); computational complexity not analyzed; identifies predictive shifts only, not causal mechanisms, limiting scientific interpretability.

Real-data validation scope: Only 3 healthcare datasets limits domain diversity; COVID-19 and Lupus findings validated post-hoc against known biology rather than against ground-truth shifted features; ACS income dataset results mentioned but insufficiently detailed.

Heuristic penalty calibration (Appendix F) relies on orthogonal design assumption that may not hold for correlated features; well-specification assumption in Eq. 1 is strong with violation modes not discussed; degradation under poor source model h_S not analyzed.

strengths: Principled reformulation of concept shift attribution as learning a sparse correction term, circumventing error accumulation issues in plugin approaches
Solid theoretical contributions with estimation consistency guarantees (Theorem 3.1-3.2) and false discovery control (Theorem 3.3) under stated assumptions
Comprehensive semi-synthetic evaluation across 48 settings covering sparse/dense shifts, high-dimensional, correlated features, low SNR, and interaction shifts
Practical efficiency demonstrated: accurate feature identification with ~100 target samples; method works robustly despite dense shifts violating sparsity assumption
Three method variants (SGShift/SGShift-A/SGShift-K) with clear tradeoffs between joint correction-selection, robustness to source misfit, and statistical guarantees
Real data case studies yield clinically/biologically plausible features (respiratory failure in COVID-19 Omicron, ancestry-specific genes in Lupus) supported by literature
weaknesses: Sparsity assumption inadequately justified: no empirical validation on real data before designing sparse method; Table 1 shows SGShift works on dense shifts, undermining core motivation; missing guidance on when method is appropriate

Real data validation lacks ground truth: COVID-19 case relies on post-hoc validation against domain knowledge without held-out test sets or false positive evaluation; Lupus case with 6 selected genes lacks independent validation; ACS experiments show sparse recovery but not that sparse updates improve generalization

Semi-synthetic experimental setup unrealistic: evaluates on known, well-behaved shifts for specific features, while real concept shifts are often heterogeneous, entangled, and ambiguous; circular evaluation—method designed for sparsity then tested on sparse shifts

Theory-practice gap on model specification: Theorem 3.1 assumes g(E_T[Y|X]) = h_S(X) + φ(X)^T δ* (well-specified correction) but never verified; if h_S poorly fit on source, learned correction conflates source misfit with true shift; assumes λ ≍ √(log K/n_T) but uses cross-validation in practice

Key theoretical assumptions not stated upfront: sub-Gaussian features, local RSC, convex loss buried in theorem; local RSC holds only around δ* (circular reasoning); no exact support recovery guarantee, only estimation consistency; Appendix F heuristic assumes orthogonal design (unrealistic)

Knockoff approach has statistical limitations: FDR control requires correction-null sign-flip property which may not hold under correlation; Appendix E shows FDR ~0.10 in some cases; Table 1 reports AUC but formal FDR control shows degraded performance; sensitivity to number of repeats and threshold π unclear

Limited real-world distinguishability of shift types: method designed for concept shift but cannot distinguish from label/covariate shift; IPW justification in Section 4.2 is post-hoc; unlabeled target data cannot be handled

Incomplete methodological clarity: three variants with overlapping objectives make it unclear when to use which; why absorption term necessary if Δ naturally absorbs source misfit on target domain?; notation inconsistencies between Δ_g(x) and Δ̂(X); only 60-90% FDR control in Table Appendix E

Weak baseline comparisons: Diff and SHAP are strawman methods not designed for concept shift; WhyShift is main competitor but no qualitative comparison of selected features or quantified error accumulation; missing domain adaptation and causal discovery baselines

Reproducibility and practical concerns: code availability not mentioned; λ selection via CV has no theoretical analysis; Appendix F heuristic unrealistic; interaction term specification robust (Appendix K) but requires basis function choices; sensitivity analysis missing on λ selection, knockoff stability, and source model misspecification severity

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing concept shift, documented as primary cause of model failure in practice
Elegant correction-based formulation avoids error accumulation of plugin approaches and works better with limited target data
Strong theoretical contributions: estimation consistency (Thm 3.1-3.2) and FDR control (Thm 3.3) under standard high-dimensional assumptions
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 48 semi-synthetic settings, diverse scenarios (sparse/dense/high-dim/correlated), AUC >0.9 substantially outperforming baselines by 0.1-0.2
Robust empirical performance: identifies 50%+ features with only 100 target samples; handles dense shifts despite sparsity assumption
Real-world validation on medical data (COVID-19, Lupus, readmission) with findings consistent with medical/biological literature
Three well-designed variants (SGShift, SGShift-A, SGShift-K) with increasing sophistication for practical flexibility
Simultaneously enables both feature attribution and performance recovery
Clear, well-organized presentation with comprehensive appendices
weaknesses: Limited to tabular data; no discussion of extension to images, graphs, or text data, substantially restricting applicability
Core sparsity assumption is unverifiable in practice; no diagnostic tools provided to check when assumption holds; unclear what fraction of real concept shifts are sparse
Theory assumes well-specified model (Eq. 1) but practice may violate this; gap between theory assumptions and empirical application not thoroughly addressed

Source model quality dependency not systematically studied; SGShift-A requires tuning λω with only heuristic guidance (range 0.1-0.9); unclear how source model misspecification affects shifted feature identification

Real data validation lacks ground truth; COVID-19/Lupus findings validated post-hoc through literature review rather than prospectively; line between predictive and causal features blurs in presentation
Baseline comparisons limited; only WhyShift as main related work; Diff and SHAP are somewhat orthogonal/repurposed methods; missing recent domain adaptation and distribution shift literature
Hyperparameter selection via cross-validation may be unreliable with small target samples; heuristic penalty calibration (Appendix F) assumes orthogonal design and homoscedasticity
Assumption verification in practice not addressed; no diagnostic tools for verifying sub-Gaussianity or restricted eigenvalue conditions; no guidance when assumptions appear violated
Limited discussion of failure modes; unclear when method would underperform or sparsity assumption breaks down; no analysis of shifts in high-order interactions only
Interaction basis specification lacks guidance; Appendix K shows robustness but limited discussion of how to choose interactions in practice
Computational complexity not discussed; SGShift-K requires B knockoff samples but runtime analysis absent
FDR control results show power loss (e.g., 0.50 power in some cases) but trade-off between control and power not deeply explored
Robustness to measurement error in target domain not addressed; only covariate/label shift tested
